text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Kerr, and may it please the court. TxDOT asked this court to reverse the trial court's denial of TxDOT's plea to the jurisdiction and render judgment for TxDOT because all actions complained of were discretionary and therefore TxDOT's immunity remains intact. Additionally, the record shows there was no condition or use of tangible property sufficient to waive TxDOT's immunity, nor was there a premises defect or a special defect. There was no proximate cause by the placement of the circular traffic signal, the green solid ball at the intersection, and finally, the state was entitled to and did in fact follow its own manual on uniform traffic control devices. TxDOT retains its sovereign immunity because all acts complained of were design-related and therefore discretionary. As you're aware, the Texas Tort Claims Act in section 101.056 protects governmental entities from that type of discretionary decision. Texas courts have long held that TxDOT enjoys immunity for its design decisions, including the choice of which traffic control device it uses on its roadways. Here, TxDOT's decision to place the circular green ball signal was discretionary and therefore immune. In order to overcome TxDOT's immunity for these discretionary decisions, Ms. Galloway must show waiver some other way. First, the condition of the intersection where the green circular ball signal was placed was not a premises defect. It's not a condition or use of tangible property. Ms. Galloway tries to circumvent the heightened standard for premises liability claims by reframing her claim as a condition or use of tangible property. That's because, of course, it's easier to demonstrate this type of thing than it is to meet the premises defect elements. The use of the circular green ball was not a condition or use of the property, nor was the sag in the road that is also complained of. But really, Ms. Galloway's complaints aren't about the circular green signal or the sag in the highway. It's more about this limited visibility that was caused by the topography in the area. But limited visibility is not a condition or use of property. For example, no TxDOT employee was putting any tangible property to use at the time of the accident, nor was it in any kind of defective condition. If you look at the Samson case that I believe both parties have cited, in which a University of Texas professor tripped over an extension cord that was extended over a sidewalk, he attempted to bring that as a condition or use of property case. And instead, the court held it's not a condition or use of property, rather it's a premises defect. Because Mr. Samson could not demonstrate that the University of Texas had actual knowledge of that condition, he couldn't demonstrate a premises defect. Active use of tangible property must be shown to waive the state's immunity. If the property simply provides an instrumentality for a condition to occur, that's not enough to make an accident more likely and therefore waive TxDOT's immunity. There was no condition or use of real property at issue here. Or pardon me, so Ms. Galloway must demonstrate instead a premises defect, but she cannot do that. To show a premises defect, she would have to show that there was an unreasonably dangerous condition of which TxDOT knew and she did not, or pardon me, her parents did not, and that the government failed to warn of that condition or make it safe.
